summary: History of US payday lending, from 19th-century salary lenders and mob loan sharks to Scott Tucker's tribal-shell empire charging up to 1,000 percent interest, plus industry-funded research and the 2019 rollback of federal rules.

evidence.note: payday-style salary lending traced to the late 1800s as regular paychecks spread
chattel mortgage lenders after the Civil War set the earliest covered period
mafia loan sharks and their rates and collection methods get several minutes
1978 Supreme Court ruling lets banks export home-state rates; start of modern industry
extended discussion of delayed wages as the root cause of the need for loans
Scott Tucker biography begins: born 1962 in Kansas City, early loan fraud
Tucker meets Hallinan in 1997 and secretly diverts their joint business
operations run from Overland Park, Kansas while posing as tribal businesses
payday money floods wealthy Mission Hills parish while poor parishes lose homes
industry lawyer steers supposedly independent academic studies
CFPB scraps Obama-era payday rules shortly before the 2019 release

notes: Primary subject is the industry as a practice, so no roles. Tucker is secondary despite a long segment (the host says he was meant to be the sole subject). covered_span starts at an estimated 1865 (post-Civil War chattel lenders; late 1800s). main_span end null since the industry is still active. labor-exploitation rests on the delayed-pay framing; Blaine Tucker's suicide is mentioned only briefly, so no warning.
